kanji.mnemonic: A single flat stroke — one finger laid on the table.
kanji.sentence: {一人|ひとり}で{東京|とうきょう}へ{行|い}きました。
kanji.translation: I went to Tokyo on my own.
kanji.usage: Japanese has two counting systems: いち、に、さん… from Chinese, and native ひとつ、ふたつ… for counting things up to ten.

kanji.mnemonic: Two lines stacked — the longer bottom one is a shelf holding up the top.
kanji.sentence: {猫|ねこ}が{二匹|にひき}います。
kanji.usage: One and two people are irregular: 一人 ひとり, 二人 ふたり. From three on it's number + にん.

kanji.mnemonic: Three lines — count them. The middle one is the shortest.
kanji.sentence: りんごを{三|みっ}つください。
kanji.usage: Months are simply number + 月: 三月 is March, the end of the Japanese school and business year.

kanji.mnemonic: A room (囗) with legs (儿) inside: four walls, four corners.
kanji.sentence: {四月|しがつ}に{日本|にほん}へ{行|い}きます。
kanji.translation: I'm going to Japan in April.
kanji.usage: し sounds like 死 (death), so よん is usually preferred — some buildings even skip room 4.

kanji.mnemonic: Between a sky line and a ground line, a figure twists like a 5 written in a hurry.
kanji.sentence: {毎朝|まいあさ}{五時|ごじ}に{起|お}きます。
kanji.translation: I get up at five every morning.
kanji.usage: Early May has Golden Week, a cluster of national holidays when much of Japan travels.

kanji.mnemonic: A lid (亠) over spread legs (八): a little hut where six people huddle.
kanji.sentence: {会議|かいぎ}は{六時|ろくじ}からです。
kanji.usage: Sounds merge in numbers: ろく + ひゃく becomes ろっぴゃく.

kanji.mnemonic: An upside-down 7 with a line through it, like a European-style seven.
kanji.sentence: {毎朝|まいあさ}{七時|しちじ}に{家|いえ}を{出|で}ます。
kanji.translation: I leave home at seven every morning.
kanji.usage: なな is often used instead of しち, because しち is easy to mishear as いち.

kanji.mnemonic: Two strokes spreading apart like the foot of a mountain.
kanji.sentence: {八時|はちじ}に{学校|がっこう}へ{行|い}きます。
kanji.translation: I go to school at eight.
kanji.usage: 八 widens toward the bottom (末広がり, 'spreading toward the end'), so it's considered a lucky number.

kanji.mnemonic: A slanted arm (丿) and a hooked elbow (乙) reaching for the ninth cookie.
kanji.sentence: {九月|くがつ}はまだ{暑|あつ}いです。
kanji.usage: く sounds like 苦 (suffering), so like 4 it's sometimes avoided. Times always use く: 九時 くじ.

kanji.mnemonic: A plus sign: two hands of five fingers crossed together make ten.
kanji.sentence: {十分|じゅっぷん}{待|ま}ってください。
kanji.usage: 十分 can be じゅっぷん (ten minutes) or じゅうぶん (enough) — context decides.

kanji.phonetic: 白 (ハク) hints at the sound ヒャク
kanji.mnemonic: One (一) over white (白): live to a hundred and everything turns white.
kanji.sentence: このペンは{百円|ひゃくえん}です。
kanji.usage: Sounds shift after some numbers: 三百 さんびゃく, 六百 ろっぴゃく, 八百 はっぴゃく.

kanji.mnemonic: Ten (十) wearing a slanted cap (丿): ten, multiplied up to a thousand.
kanji.sentence: {千円|せんえん}{札|さつ}しかありません。
kanji.usage: Large numbers are grouped by 万 (10,000), not by thousands: 10,000 is 一万 いちまん.

kanji.mnemonic: A shop window frame with a bar across it — the price tag says yen.
kanji.sentence: このケーキは{五百円|ごひゃくえん}です。
kanji.usage: Both ¥ and 円 are read えん. 百円ショップ (100-yen shops) sell almost everything.

kanji.mnemonic: The sun, once drawn as a circle with a dot, squared off over time.
kanji.sentence: {今日|きょう}は{日曜日|にちようび}です。
kanji.usage: Shop hours often list 日・祝, meaning 'Sundays and holidays'. 今日 is read きょう as a whole word — a special reading.

kanji.mnemonic: A crescent moon with two wisps of cloud drifting across it.
kanji.sentence: {今夜|こんや}は{月|つき}がきれいですね。
kanji.translation: The moon is beautiful tonight, isn't it?
kanji.usage: 月がきれいですね is famously — if probably apocryphally — credited to Natsume Sōseki as a subtle way to say 'I love you'.

kanji.mnemonic: A campfire: flames leaping up with sparks flying out on both sides.
kanji.sentence: {火|ひ}に{気|き}をつけてください。
kanji.usage: 花火 (fireworks, literally 'flower fire') are the highlight of summer festivals.

kanji.mnemonic: A main stream running down the middle with splashes to the left and right.
kanji.sentence: {水|みず}を{一杯|いっぱい}ください。
kanji.usage: Restaurants bring お水 (water, with the polite お) free of charge.

kanji.mnemonic: A trunk with branches reaching up and roots spreading below.
kanji.sentence: {公園|こうえん}に{大|おお}きい{木|き}があります。
kanji.translation: There's a big tree in the park.
kanji.usage: 木 appears in many surnames: 木村, 鈴木, 佐々木.

kanji.mnemonic: Under a roof (人), a king (王) guards two glittering nuggets of gold.
kanji.sentence: {金曜日|きんようび}に{友|とも}だちと{会|あ}います。
kanji.translation: I'm meeting a friend on Friday.
kanji.usage: In everyday speech money is お金, with the polite prefix お.

kanji.mnemonic: A cross planted in a mound — the bottom line is the ground, wider than the top.
kanji.sentence: {土曜日|どようび}は{休|やす}みです。
kanji.usage: Calendars mark the week with one kanji per day: 月 火 水 木 金 土 日 — the moon, five elements and the sun.

kanji.mnemonic: A person bent under a sheaf of harvested grain — one harvest, one year.
kanji.sentence: {来年|らいねん}、{日本|にほん}に{住|す}みたいです。
kanji.translation: Next year, I want to live in Japan.
kanji.usage: Japan also counts years by imperial era: 2019 was 令和元年, the first year of Reiwa.

kanji.phonetic: 寺 (ジ) gives the sound ジ
kanji.mnemonic: Sun (日) + temple (寺): the temple bell rings by the sun to tell the time.
kanji.sentence: {今|いま}、{何時|なんじ}ですか。
kanji.usage: Watch the irregular hours: 四時 よじ, 七時 しちじ, 九時 くじ.

kanji.mnemonic: Someone ducks under a roof (人) right now — the rain has just started.
kanji.sentence: {今日|きょう}は{忙|いそが}しいです。
kanji.usage: 今日 (きょう) and 今年 (ことし) are whole-word readings — learn them as words, not kanji by kanji.

kanji.phonetic: 可 (カ) gives the sound カ
kanji.mnemonic: A person (亻) sees something that might be possible (可) and asks: what?
kanji.sentence: これは{何|なん}ですか。
kanji.usage: なに becomes なん before d-, n- and t- sounds and before counters: 何ですか, 何時, 何人.

kanji.mnemonic: Antlers on top, then flesh (月) and a knife (刂): the hunter always walks in front.
kanji.sentence: {駅|えき}の{前|まえ}で{待|ま}っています。
kanji.translation: I'm waiting in front of the station.
kanji.usage: 駅前 ('in front of the station') is the classic meeting spot in every Japanese town.

kanji.mnemonic: Stepping (彳) with a thread (幺) tangled round slow feet (夂) — you fall behind.
kanji.sentence: {仕事|しごと}の{後|あと}で{会|あ}いましょう。
kanji.usage: In speech, times use 午前 (a.m.) and 午後 (p.m.); printed timetables usually use the 24-hour clock.

kanji.mnemonic: Two legs mid-stride: a person seen from the side.
kanji.sentence: あの{人|ひと}は{先生|せんせい}です。
kanji.usage: Nationality is country + 人 (じん): アメリカ人, 日本人. Counting people is number + 人 (にん).

kanji.mnemonic: A baby swaddled in a blanket, arms stretched out wide (一).
kanji.sentence: {子|こ}どもが{公園|こうえん}で{遊|あそ}んでいます。
kanji.translation: Children are playing in the park.
kanji.usage: 子 was a classic ending for women's given names of earlier generations: 花子, 洋子.

kanji.mnemonic: A figure kneeling gracefully with arms crossed.
kanji.sentence: {女|おんな}の{人|ひと}が{歌|うた}っています。
kanji.usage: Look for 女 on toilet and bath signs. At hot springs, the curtain marked 女湯 is the women's bath.

kanji.mnemonic: Power (力) in the rice field (田): the field worker.
kanji.sentence: {男|おとこ}の{子|こ}が{走|はし}っています。
kanji.usage: At hot springs, 男湯 is the men's bath. 男性 and 女性 are the polite forms you'll see on forms and signs.

kanji.mnemonic: A foot stepping out ahead of a pair of legs (儿) — the one who went first.
kanji.sentence: {先週|せんしゅう}、{京都|きょうと}へ{行|い}きました。
kanji.translation: Last week I went to Kyoto.
kanji.usage: 先生 is also the title for doctors, lawyers and politicians. お先に失礼します ('excuse me for leaving first') is said when leaving work before colleagues.

kanji.mnemonic: A sprout pushing up through the ground (土) — life being born.
kanji.sentence: {私|わたし}は{大学生|だいがくせい}です。
kanji.usage: 生 has more readings than almost any other kanji, so learn it word by word: 生ビール (なま, draft beer), 一生 (いっしょう, a lifetime).

kanji.mnemonic: A child (子) under a roof with three sparks of knowledge above — the schoolhouse.
kanji.sentence: {日本語|にほんご}を{学|まな}んでいます。
kanji.usage: In 学校, がく + こう becomes がっこう: the く shrinks to a small っ. You'll see this sound change everywhere.

kanji.mnemonic: Evening (夕) + mouth (口): in the dark you call out your name so people know who you are.
kanji.sentence: お{名前|なまえ}は{何|なん}ですか。
kanji.usage: Family names come first in Japanese: in 山田太郎, Yamada is the family name. Business cards (名刺) are offered and received with both hands.

kanji.mnemonic: Two hands (ナ and 又) reaching for each other — friends.
kanji.sentence: {友|とも}だちと{映画|えいが}を{見|み}ました。
kanji.translation: I watched a film with a friend.
kanji.usage: 友だち is everyday; 友人 sounds formal and appears in writing and speeches. Same meaning, different register.

kanji.mnemonic: A line rising up from the ground line.
kanji.sentence: {机|つくえ}の{上|うえ}に{本|ほん}があります。
kanji.translation: There's a book on the desk.
kanji.usage: Learners hear 日本語が上手ですね a lot. The modest reply is いいえ、まだまだです ('no, I still have a long way to go').

kanji.mnemonic: A line hanging down from the ceiling line.
kanji.sentence: {椅子|いす}の{下|した}に{猫|ねこ}がいます。
kanji.translation: There's a cat under the chair.
kanji.usage: On railways, 上り trains run toward Tokyo or the main city, and 下り trains run away from it.

kanji.mnemonic: A box (口) pierced straight through the middle.
kanji.sentence: かばんの{中|なか}に{何|なに}がありますか。
kanji.usage: Shop signs: 営業中 means 'open', 準備中 means 'getting ready' (closed). Here 中 means 'in the middle of'.

kanji.mnemonic: A person stretching their arms wide: 'it was THIS big!'
kanji.sentence: {大|おお}きい{家|いえ}ですね。
kanji.usage: Menus often offer 大盛り (おおもり), a large serving, next to the regular size.

kanji.mnemonic: One tiny stroke in the middle with two little drops beside it.
kanji.sentence: {小|ちい}さい{犬|いぬ}が{好|す}きです。
kanji.usage: As a prefix, 小 can mean small or slight: 小雨 (こさめ) is a light drizzle.

kanji.mnemonic: A hand (ナ) bringing food to the mouth (口) — most people eat with their right hand.
kanji.sentence: {次|つぎ}の{角|かど}を{右|みぎ}に{曲|ま}がってください。
kanji.translation: Please turn right at the next corner.
kanji.usage: In Tokyo, people stand on the left of escalators; in Osaka, on the right.

kanji.mnemonic: A hand (ナ) steadying a tool (工) — the left hand holds while the right one works.
kanji.sentence: {左|ひだり}に{銀行|ぎんこう}があります。
kanji.translation: There's a bank on the left.
kanji.usage: Cars drive on the left in Japan, so look right first when you cross the road.

kanji.mnemonic: Three peaks, the middle one the tallest.
kanji.sentence: {富士山|ふじさん}に{登|のぼ}りたいです。
kanji.translation: I want to climb Mt. Fuji.
kanji.usage: Mountain names use the on'yomi: 富士山 is ふじさん, never 'Fuji-yama'.

kanji.mnemonic: Three streams of water flowing down side by side.
kanji.sentence: {川|かわ}で{泳|およ}ぎました。
kanji.usage: After another word, かわ often softens to がわ: 小川 おがわ, 品川 しながわ.

kanji.mnemonic: A line (一) above a big person (大): what's above your head is the sky.
kanji.sentence: {明日|あした}の{天気|てんき}はどうですか。
kanji.usage: 天気予報 (てんきよほう), the weather forecast, is a fixture of morning TV.

kanji.mnemonic: Steam (气) rising with a swirl (メ) inside: energy, spirit, the air around you.
kanji.sentence: お{元気|げんき}ですか。
kanji.usage: お元気ですか is for someone you haven't seen in a while — it isn't a daily 'how are you'.

kanji.mnemonic: Four raindrops falling from a cloud that hangs under the sky line.
kanji.sentence: {雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}っています。
kanji.usage: 梅雨 (つゆ), the rainy season, soaks most of Japan in June and July.

kanji.mnemonic: A tree (木) with a line marking its root: the origin — and books are the root of knowledge.
kanji.sentence: {毎晩|まいばん}、{本|ほん}を{読|よ}みます。
kanji.usage: 本 also counts long, thin things — pens, bottles, trains: 一本 いっぽん, 二本 にほん, 三本 さんぼん.

kanji.mnemonic: A person (亻) leaning against a tree (木): taking a rest.

words.meaning: to rest; to take time off

kanji.sentence: {少|すこ}し{休|やす}みましょう。
kanji.usage: Shop signs: 定休日 is the regular closing day; 本日休業 means 'closed today'.

kanji.mnemonic: An eye (目) on legs (儿), walking around to see everything.
kanji.sentence: {窓|まど}から{海|うみ}が{見|み}えます。
kanji.translation: You can see the sea from the window.
kanji.usage: In shops, 見せてください ('please show me') is how you ask to look at an item.

kanji.mnemonic: A crossroads seen from above: which way will you go?
kanji.sentence: {明日|あした}、{銀行|ぎんこう}に{行|い}きます。
kanji.translation: I'm going to the bank tomorrow.
kanji.usage: On train displays, 東京行 means 'bound for Tokyo'.

kanji.mnemonic: A tree (木) with a crossbar: once a drawing of wheat, a crop that came from far away.
kanji.sentence: {友|とも}だちが{家|いえ}に{来|き}ました。
kanji.translation: A friend came over to my place.
kanji.usage: 来る is irregular: 来ます (きます), 来ない (こない), 来て (きて).

kanji.mnemonic: A lid (人) over something good (良): a covered dish of good food.
kanji.sentence: {朝|あさ}ご{飯|はん}を{食|た}べましたか。
kanji.usage: Say いただきます before eating and ごちそうさまでした afterwards — both are expected at the table.

kanji.mnemonic: Words (言) + tongue (舌): talking.
kanji.sentence: {母|はは}と{電話|でんわ}で{話|はな}しました。
kanji.translation: I talked with my mother on the phone.
kanji.usage: Casual calls open with もしもし. In business calls you give your company and name first.

kanji.phonetic: 吾 (ゴ) gives the sound ゴ
kanji.mnemonic: Words (言) + I (吾): the words I speak — my language.
kanji.sentence: {英語|えいご}と{日本語|にほんご}が{話|はな}せます。
kanji.translation: I can speak English and Japanese.
kanji.usage: Country + 語 gives its language: 中国語, 韓国語. English is 英語, from 英 for England.

kanji.mnemonic: Words (言) + sell (売): a news-seller reading the headlines aloud.
kanji.sentence: {新聞|しんぶん}を{読|よ}みますか。
kanji.usage: 読み方 is the word to use when you ask how a kanji is read: この漢字の読み方は？

kanji.phonetic: 交 (コウ) gives the sound コウ
kanji.mnemonic: Tree (木) + mix (交): children mixing together under the trees of the schoolyard.
kanji.sentence: {学校|がっこう}は{八時半|はちじはん}に{始|はじ}まります。
kanji.translation: School starts at half past eight.
kanji.usage: The Japanese school year begins in April, under the cherry blossoms.

kanji.mnemonic: A cart seen from above: an axle through the middle with a wheel at each end.
kanji.sentence: {車|くるま}で{会社|かいしゃ}に{行|い}きます。
kanji.usage: 車 on its own means a car; trains are 電車, 'electric vehicles'.

kanji.mnemonic: Under the rain clouds (雨), a lightning bolt with a hooked tail strikes: electricity.
kanji.sentence: {電車|でんしゃ}が{来|き}ました。
kanji.usage: 電 means electricity in nearly every word — 'turn off the light' is 電気を消して.

kanji.mnemonic: A rice field divided into four neat plots.
kanji.sentence: {田中|たなか}さんは{田|た}んぼで{働|はたら}いています。
kanji.translation: Tanaka-san works in the rice paddies.
kanji.usage: Rice paddies shaped many surnames: 田中 ('in the fields'), 山田 ('mountain field').

kanji.mnemonic: Three tiers of new growth and a person stretching under the sun (日): spring.
kanji.sentence: {春|はる}になると、{桜|さくら}が{咲|さ}きます。
kanji.translation: When spring comes, the cherry blossoms bloom.
kanji.usage: The school and business year starts in April, so spring means fresh starts.

kanji.mnemonic: A heavy head on top, slow dragging feet (夂) below: too hot to hurry in summer.
kanji.sentence: {夏休|なつやす}みに{海|うみ}へ{行|い}きました。
kanji.translation: I went to the beach during the summer holidays.
kanji.usage: Summer is festival (祭り) season: yukata, fireworks and street food.

kanji.mnemonic: Grain (禾) + fire (火): fields are harvested and the stubble is burned — autumn.
kanji.sentence: {秋|あき}は{食|た}べ{物|もの}がおいしいです。
kanji.usage: Autumn is called 食欲の秋, 'the season of appetite', for its harvest foods.

kanji.mnemonic: Slow feet (夂) shuffling over two flakes of ice: winter.
kanji.sentence: {冬|ふゆ}は{雪|ゆき}が{降|ふ}ります。
kanji.usage: In winter, families gather around a こたつ — a low heated table covered with a quilt.

lines.jp: {東京|とうきょう}{行|ゆ}き　{九時|くじ}{十分|じゅっぷん}{発|はつ}
lines.en: Bound for Tokyo — departs 9:10

lines.jp: まもなく、{一番線|いちばんせん}に{電車|でんしゃ}が{参|まい}ります。
lines.en: A train will shortly arrive at platform 1.

lines.jp: {黄色|きいろ}い{線|せん}の{内側|うちがわ}までお{下|さ}がりください。
lines.en: Please stand behind the yellow line.

lines.jp: {電車|でんしゃ}の{中|なか}では、{電話|でんわ}はご{遠慮|えんりょ}ください。
lines.en: Please refrain from phone calls on the train.

lines.jp: {出口|でぐち}は{左|ひだり}です。
lines.en: The exit is on the left.

notes.text: Signs drop verbs and particles: 東京行き 九時十分発 is just two noun phrases. Public signage favors this compact style.
Announcements use keigo: 参ります (humble 'comes'), お下がりください, ご遠慮ください ('kindly refrain'). You'll rarely say these yourself, but you'll hear them every day.
Talking on the phone in trains is considered rude in Japan. People switch to マナーモード (silent mode) and text instead.

question.prompt: What are passengers asked not to do on the train?
question.explanation: 電話はご遠慮ください means 'please refrain from phone calls'.

lines.jp: {日本|にほん}には{春|はる}、{夏|なつ}、{秋|あき}、{冬|ふゆ}の{四|よっ}つの{季節|きせつ}があります。
lines.en: Japan has four seasons: spring, summer, autumn and winter.

lines.jp: {春|はる}は{桜|さくら}の{下|した}で{花見|はなみ}をします。
lines.en: In spring, people hold flower-viewing parties under the cherry trees.

lines.jp: {夏|なつ}は{暑|あつ}くて、{雨|あめ}もたくさん{降|ふ}ります。
lines.en: Summer is hot, and it rains a lot too.

lines.jp: {秋|あき}になると、{山|やま}の{木|き}が{赤|あか}くなります。
lines.en: When autumn comes, the trees on the mountains turn red.

lines.jp: {冬|ふゆ}は{寒|さむ}いですが、{雪|ゆき}の{山|やま}はとてもきれいです。
lines.en: Winter is cold, but the snowy mountains are beautiful.

notes.text: Seasonal awareness (季節感) runs through Japanese life: food, greetings and even business letters open with a nod to the season.
Each sentence opens with a season + は. Repeating the same topic frame is a simple way a Japanese paragraph signals a list.
New words are built from kanji you know: 花 (flower) + 見 (see) = 花見, 'flower viewing'.

question.prompt: What happens to the mountain trees in autumn?
question.explanation: 山の木が赤くなります: 'the mountain trees turn red'.

lines.speaker: {店員|てんいん}
lines.jp: いらっしゃいませ。{何名様|なんめいさま}ですか。
lines.en: Welcome! How many in your party?

lines.speaker: {客|きゃく}
lines.jp: {二人|ふたり}です。
lines.en: Two.

lines.speaker: {店員|てんいん}
lines.jp: こちらへどうぞ。
lines.en: This way, please.

lines.speaker: {客|きゃく}
lines.jp: すみません、お{水|みず}をください。
lines.en: Excuse me, could we have some water?

lines.speaker: {店員|てんいん}
lines.jp: はい、{少々|しょうしょう}お{待|ま}ちください。
lines.en: Certainly — one moment, please.

lines.speaker: {客|きゃく}
lines.jp: ごちそうさまでした。
lines.en: Thank you for the meal.

notes.text: いらっしゃいませ is a greeting that expects no reply — a small nod is enough. A question like 何名様ですか opens an adjacency pair: the answer comes right away, usually short (二人です).
Staff speak in keigo (何名様, 少々お待ちください) while customers use plain polite です/ください. The asymmetry is normal in Japanese service encounters.
There's no tipping in Japan. Saying ごちそうさまでした as you leave is the thanks.

question.prompt: How many people are in the customer's group?
question.explanation: 二人です: 'two people'. 二人 is read ふたり.

lines.jp: {十月|じゅうがつ}{五日|いつか}　{雨|あめ}
lines.en: October 5th — rain

lines.jp: {今日|きょう}は{学校|がっこう}が{休|やす}みだった。
lines.en: There was no school today.

lines.jp: {朝|あさ}、{友|とも}だちと{電話|でんわ}で{話|はな}した。
lines.en: In the morning, I talked to a friend on the phone.

lines.jp: {午後|ごご}は{本|ほん}を{読|よ}んで、{日本|にほん}の{映画|えいが}を{見|み}た。
lines.en: In the afternoon, I read a book and watched a Japanese film.

lines.jp: {明日|あした}は{山田|やまだ}{先生|せんせい}の{授業|じゅぎょう}だ。{早|はや}く{寝|ね}よう。
lines.en: Tomorrow is Professor Yamada's class. I'll get to bed early.

notes.text: Diaries use the plain form (だった, 話した, 見た). With no listener to be polite to, です/ます would sound oddly formal.
Dates are month + day. Days 1–10 use native readings: 五日 is いつか, not ごにち.
Teachers are addressed as surname + 先生 — never by their first name, even outside class.

question.prompt: What did the writer do in the afternoon?
options: Read a book and watched a film
question.explanation: 午後は本を読んで、日本の映画を見た。

lines.jp: {山田|やまだ}{先生|せんせい}
lines.en: Professor Yamada,

lines.jp: いつもお{世話|せわ}になっております。{一年|いちねん}のキムです。
lines.en: Thank you, as always, for your guidance. This is Kim, first year.

lines.jp: {熱|ねつ}があるので、{明日|あした}は{学校|がっこう}を{休|やす}みます。
lines.en: I have a fever, so I'll be absent from school tomorrow.

lines.jp: {申|もう}し{訳|わけ}ありません。
lines.en: I'm very sorry.

lines.jp: よろしくお{願|ねが}いします。
lines.en: Thank you for your understanding.

notes.text: Formal emails open with a set phrase (いつもお世話になっております) and close with よろしくお願いします. Leaving them out sounds abrupt rather than efficient.
Apologizing for an absence — even with a good reason — maintains the relationship. It isn't an admission of fault.
The structure is fixed: name → greeting → who you are → reason → apology → closing. Learn the frame once and you can write many emails.

question.prompt: Why will Kim miss school tomorrow?
question.explanation: 熱があるので: 'because I have a fever'.

confusions.tip: 人 (person): the left stroke sits on top. 入 (enter): the right stroke sits on top, like an arrow pointing in.
大 is big. A dot at the top right makes 犬 (dog); a dot at the bottom makes 太 (thick); a line on top makes 天 (sky).
日 has one inner line, 目 (eye) has two, 白 (white) adds a tick on top, and 田 (field) is split into four.
土 (earth): the bottom line is longer — the ground is wide. 士 (samurai): the top line is longer.
Both start with a hand (ナ). 右 has a mouth 口; 左 has a tool 工. Their stroke order differs too: 右 starts with the slanted stroke, 左 with the horizontal one.
木 is a tree. 本 adds a line at the root. 休 is a person resting against a 木; 体 (body) has 本 instead.
十 is ten. 千 (thousand) adds a slanted stroke on top; 干 (dry) has a flat line on top instead.
見 (see) ends in walking legs 儿; 貝 (shellfish) ends in two short strokes like little feet.
All three start with 言 (words). The right side tells them apart: 舌 tongue → 話 talk, 吾 → 語 language, 売 → 読 read.
学 (study) has three short marks on top; 字 (character) has a plain roof 宀.
小 (small) is three strokes; 少 (few) adds a long sweeping stroke at the bottom.
